source: Wang et al. (2025) Hilbert: recursively building formal proofs with informal reasoning
finding: Depth ablation: with no decomposition (D=0) the standalone Goedel-Prover-V2-32B pass@4 gets 75% on miniF2F; with recursive subgoal decomposition by Gemini 2.5 Pro, 98.36% at D=2 and 98.7% at D=3. Turning off the informal shallow solve needs more depth for the same result.
numbers: miniF2F, Gemini 2.5 Pro + Goedel-Prover-V2-32B: D=0 75%, D=2 98.36%, D=3 98.7%.
quote: The consistent improvement over the D = 0 baseline (75% pass rate) validates the efficacy of hierarchical subgoal decomposition
limits: D=0 is a pass@4 prover with no informal reasoner and far fewer tokens. It is not an equal-token control, so it cannot separate decomposition from extra compute or from the stronger Gemini reasoner.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays partly open: decomposition clearly helps, but the paper gives no same-token direct arm.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Hilbert, Table 1 and Table 3
finding: Hilbert's gain over direct proving is confounded with adding a strong informal reasoner. The same Goedel-32B prover alone reaches 90.8% at pass@8192 and 94.7% with self-correction at pass@1024. Hilbert reaches 99.2%. Gemini 2.5 Pro alone is 49.1% (pass@16384, quoted from another paper). A 7B DeepSeek prover goes from 61.3% (pass@4) to 96.7% or 98.4% inside Hilbert, above the 671B model at pass@8192 (88.9%).
numbers: miniF2F-test. Hilbert average tokens per decomposed sample with Goedel-32B and retrieval: 2.3M reasoner and 1.3M prover.
limits: No arm gives the prover the same total tokens (reasoner plus prover) as Hilbert. Prover-only budgets are counted in samples, not tokens. Reasoner model (Gemini 2.5 Pro or Flash, gpt-oss-120b) differs from the prover.
agent_relevance: A scaffold gain of 4 to 8 points over a strong direct baseline is plausible, but it cannot be credited to lemmas alone. Compare at equal tokens in our own test.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Hilbert, retrieval ablation
finding: Retrieving existing library theorems raises pass rate and cuts cost. Without retrieval the model also makes wrong theorem-name errors.
numbers: miniF2F: DeepSeek 98.4% vs 97.1%, Goedel 99.2% vs 97.9%. Goedel: reasoner calls 548 vs 862, reasoner tokens 2.3M vs 4.0M. DeepSeek: reasoner tokens 1.9M vs 2.1M, prover calls 205 vs 290.
quote: retrieval improves both performance and efficiency by surfacing useful theorems that simplify proofs
limits: Retrieves existing Mathlib theorems, not newly proposed lemmas. Gain is 1.3 points near a ceiling, single run, no interval.
agent_relevance: Looking up what is already known saves tokens as well as raising accuracy. Supports a cheap check-what-exists step before conjecturing.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Hilbert, appendix A.6 compute scaling
finding: On PutnamBench the cumulative pass rate rises steadily with more reasoner calls and tokens. No equal-token direct-prover curve is drawn.
numbers: PutnamBench, Gemini 2.5 Pro: pass rate from 13.3% at the smallest budget to 55.9% at 328K reasoner calls, 424K total LLM calls, 1880M total tokens (figure labels).
limits: Values read from text extraction of plots. Main-table runs used exhaustive retries without compute tracking.
agent_relevance: Decomposition systems are compute hungry. A fair test needs the direct arm to get the same token budget, which nobody has run.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Seed-Prover: deep and broad reasoning for automated theorem proving
finding: Seed-Prover reports no ablation of lemma pool or conjecture count. It reports only settings. Light gets 201/657 on PutnamBench, medium 331/657. Heavy starts with a conjecture pool (default 5,000) and runs for days. Past IMO: 121/155 overall; 47/55 easy, 47/56 medium, 27/44 hard.
numbers: PutnamBench light 201/657, medium 331/657. Past IMO 121/155 (78.1%). Heavy was used only on post-2017 problems that medium failed.
limits: Light, medium and heavy differ in compute and in lemma use at once. Heavy is applied after medium fails, so there is no paired comparison. No curve of success against number of conjectures.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 6 stay open for Seed-Prover: no fixed-prover ablation and no breadth curve in the paper.

source: Wang et al. (2023) LEGO-Prover: neural theorem proving with growing libraries
finding: The library already has a de-duplication step: a new skill is added only if difflib SequenceMatcher similarity to existing ones is under 0.85. The library reached 22,532 skills: 10.8% from the prover, 38.2% from the evolver's request solving, 51.1% from directional transformation. The authors say some lemmas are trivial or already in Isabelle.
numbers: 22,532 skills. About 300 dollars per experiment of 100 attempts (footnote).
quote: Although some lemmas are trivially true or already exist in Isabelle's theorem library
limits: Text-similarity dedup catches near copies only. No triviality filter is evaluated and no count of how many of the 22,532 are used.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: dedup exists but its effect on the +3.3 points is not tested. Cheap dedup is easy to copy.

source: Wang et al. (2023) LEGO-Prover ablation and usage analysis
finding: The no-library arm removes both the library and the evolver, so the +3.3 points mixes the two and the evolver spends extra tokens. 24% of the 135 problems proved on miniF2F-valid used retrieved skills. Of those, 51% copied the skill directly and 49% wrote new lemmas imitating it. Directly reused skills mostly came from request solving (71%).
numbers: miniF2F-valid, 50 attempts: 50.4% vs 47.1%. 135 problems verified, 24% (about 32) with skill help. Origin of directly used skills: 71% requests, 12% key concepts, 12% scaling, 6% parameterization.
quote: many trivial problems in the dataset miniF2F can be solved trivially without requiring any skill
limits: Valid split only, one run, 50 attempts. The library is shared across problems in the run, so retrieval can cross problems, but there is no held-out split and no per-lemma cross-problem count.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open. Gap 4 narrows: LEGO does reuse across problems inside one benchmark run, but the count is small (about 32 problems) and not split by source problem.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: More samples raise coverage almost log-linearly when a verifier exists. Without a verifier the gain mostly does not convert into accuracy.
numbers: MATH, Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000. Majority vote or reward model: 40.50% to 41.41% over the same range. SWE-bench Lite: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250.
quote: tools like proof checkers and unit tests can automatically verify every sample
limits: Samples of whole answers, not lemmas. Still the right equal-token baseline for gap 1.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: the direct-attempt baseline is repeated sampling plus a verifier. In plain text, a cheap self-check decides whether lemma tokens beat extra attempts.

finding: Subgoal-decomposition style chain of thought helps but costs about ten times more output tokens. Subgoals are also turned into conjectured theorems for training.
numbers: miniF2F-test 671B non-CoT 1 sample 52.94%; CoT 82.4% at pass@32, 88.9% at pass@8192. Average output tokens non-CoT vs CoT: 7B 442.6 vs 4488.5, 671B 761.8 vs 6751.9.
limits: Gains are not at equal tokens. Table rows partly scrambled in text extraction, so the non-CoT row is read with care.
agent_relevance: Decomposition effects in formal provers come with a large token bill. Report accuracy per token.

source: Si, Yang and Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?
finding: LLM judges are weak at deciding which ideas are good. Human reviewers agree with each other only 56.1% of the time on idea ranking. The best LLM judge (their Claude-3.5 pairwise ranker) agrees with humans 53.3%. On accepted vs rejected papers Claude-3.5-Sonnet reaches 71.4% zero-shot (GPT-4o 61.1%, Claude-3-Opus 63.5%).
numbers: Human-human consistency 56.1%. Best LLM evaluator 53.3%. Paper accept/reject: 71.4%, 61.1%, 63.5%.
limits: Research ideas in NLP, not mathematical conjectures. Same direction as MathlibLemma's 46% false rejections but a different task.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: judge accuracy is near chance on novelty or quality of ideas. Prefer tool checks (proof, counterexample) to a judge model, and audit any judge on a sample.

finding: Changing only names barely moves accuracy (original GSM8K is close to the names-only distribution), but changing numbers drops it more, and both together most. Adding one irrelevant clause drops performance up to 65%. All models vary across instantiations of one question.
numbers: Names-only change: small effect. Values changed: larger drop. Extra clause: drop up to 65%.
limits: Grade-school word problems where names are irrelevant by design. Renaming tests recall only when the names carry the meaning.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: the renaming test does not carry over to word problems. Johansson and Smallbone renamed domain-bearing symbols, a stronger test. Perturb meaning-bearing names or constants instead.

finding: Programmatic variation of variables and constants in Putnam problems lowers accuracy for every model tested, which points to recall of seen problems.
numbers: 522 original problems, 100 variants. o1-preview 41.9% on original, down 19.6 points (46.8% relative) on paired variations. 19 models; 10 with non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals.
limits: Only 100 variants. Variants may also be harder, so recall is not the only reading. Answers graded by boxed result.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: a second domain where perturbing constants shows recall. Supports checking any lemma that looks too familiar by changing its constants.

source: Li et al. (2025) CounterMath: counterexample-driven conceptual reasoning
finding: Models are poor at proving or disproving statements with counterexamples. Judging true or false is better than giving a valid rationale. The authors conclude that o1-class models still have insufficient counterexample-driven proof capability.
numbers: Approximate, from a scrambled table: GPT-4o judgement F1 59.0, strict rationale about 19.7%; o1-preview F1 60.1, strict rationale about 39.8%; Gemini 2.5 Pro judgement F1 80.7, loose rationale 65.3% (row alignment uncertain).
limits: University-level, hand-made statement-judging benchmark. Row alignment in the table is uncertain, so only the pattern is reliable.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a counterexample self-check by the model is not reliable. Pair it with small-case computation by tool rather than model judgement.

finding: In plain text, asking the model to first list subproblems and solve them in order beats plain chain of thought on compositional tasks.
numbers: SCAN length split: at least 99% with 14 exemplars vs 16% with chain of thought (code-davinci-002).
limits: Decomposition into subproblems, not into reusable lemmas. Synthetic task. No equal-token comparison.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: closest plain-text evidence that staged decomposition raises correctness. It is not a lemma test.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Hilbert, no-shallow-solve variant
finding: When informal shallow solving of subgoals is disabled, the system needs greater depth to reach the same pass rate. The depth gain is partly the informal reasoner doing real work at each level.
numbers: miniF2F: full system 98.36% at D=2; the no-shallow-solve variant needs more depth for comparable results.
limits: Read from figure and text; exact variant numbers are not in the text.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: part of the decomposition gain is the reasoner, not the lemma pool.

finding: Web search quota was exhausted. This pass opened papers by direct arXiv ID only. No new paper was found that tests gaps 1, 2 (plain-text lemma truth rate), 6, 7 or 8 directly.
limits: Absence of evidence reflects the search limit as well as the literature.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 2, 6, 7, 8 should be treated as unmeasured until a later search pass.
